narrative:
The model predicts you have a 16% chance of failing your final year, which is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this decision were your number of past class failures, your desire to pursue higher education, and the quality of your family relationships. Surprisingly, having no previous failures was the strongest element pulling the prediction toward passing. Your clear ambition to continue studying beyond high school also worked in your favor, pushing the outcome away from failure. However, the model saw your family relationships as only “good” rather than very good, and this was the main factor that nudged the prediction toward failing. Compared with students who passed, you also stand out for having nine absences—more than double the average of 3.78 absences among those who succeeded.

Although the overall risk looks low, the combination of average family support and higher-than-normal absences appears to have outweighed your clean record and strong ambitions. To improve, focus on attending every class and strengthening daily study habits beyond your current less-than-two-hours per week. Talk with your family about how they can help you stay on track. These small, consistent changes can turn a borderline prediction into a clear pass.
